info.bio: Joe Meek es uno de los personajes más oscuros que engendró la música popular de la segunda mitad del ultimo siglo del milenio pasado, o sea el rock. Es complicado comenzar a escribir sobre este británico obsesionado con el ocultismo y Buddy Holly. Nació a finales de los años veinte en el suroeste de Inglaterra. Comenzó su carrera laboral con un trabajo muy por fuera de lo común: como operario de radar para las fuerzas armadas. Cuando rondaba sus veinticinco años de edad

own_scenes.desc: Productor independiente pionero en el mundo cerrado de la industria británica, trabajaba solo en un piso de Holloway Road con una compresión feroz y sonidos extraterrestres: «Johnny Remember Me» de John Leyton (1961), cantada por un hombre a un hombre, y «Telstar» de los Tornados (1962), número 1 a ambos lados del Atlántico. Sensible, casi clarividente, con un genio violento, vivió perseguido (real e imaginariamente): detenido en 1963 por «importunar» en un urinario, chantajeado, adicto a las anfetaminas, obsesionado con micrófonos ocultos, el ocultismo y los cementerios; los derechos de «Telstar» quedaron congelados por un pleito. Tras los Beatles su sonido parecía pasado. El 12 de agosto de 1966 salió el último disco de los Tornados con él, «Is That a Ship I Hear?», con olas y gaviotas para los piratas; nadie lo quiso. En la cara B, «Do You Come Here Often?», tras dos minutos de órgano, dos voces camp se pelean en un club gay de Londres: el primer disco de una gran discográfica británica con un retrato tan exacto de la vida homosexual. Su salud mental empeoró ese otoño, con deudas y amenazas de gánsteres.

refs.q: On 12 August, the Tornados released their last-ever record with Joe Meek.
refs.para: On 12 August, the Tornados released their last-ever record with Joe Meek. Beginning with the sound of waves and seagulls, ‘Is That a Ship I Hear?’ bore all its producer’s hallmarks: the boot-stomping drums, the extraterrestrial keyboard sound and fierce, fierce compression. It was constructed around a gimmick: Meek hoped that the title and the ocean effects would convince the DJs on the pirate radio stations to put his new record on heavy rotation.
refs.chapter: Agosto: Do You Come Here Often? Joe Meek, los derechos gais y un verano de violencia

refs.para: The result was a masterpiece. The scenario is a London club, quite possibly the Apollo or Le Duce. The organist is still pumping away, as he has done for the last two minutes, but that’s only background as the sound dims and the bar atmosphere comes in. The two run through their brief but diverting exchange, ending with the kiss-off:
refs.chapter: Agosto: Do You Come Here Often? Joe Meek, los derechos gais y un verano de violencia

refs.q: ‘Do You Come Here Often?’ was the first record on a UK major label – Columbia – to deliver a slice of homosexual life
refs.para: ‘Do You Come Here Often?’ was the first record on a UK major label – Columbia – to deliver a slice of homosexual life so accurate that it’s possible to hear its cut-and-thrust in any gay bar today. And, although Meek wasn’t aware of the wider implications, the hints of violence and the subcultural assertiveness contained within the track chimed exactly with both the public mood and the underlying trends of that troubled, heightened high summer.
refs.chapter: Agosto: Do You Come Here Often? Joe Meek, los derechos gais y un verano de violencia

refs.q: Meek’s moment of triumph came with the Tornados’ ‘Telstar’
refs.para: Meek’s moment of triumph came with the Tornados’ ‘Telstar’, which stayed at #1 for three weeks in the US and five in the UK. It remains as haunting and as evocative as it was over forty years ago, a triumph of technological optimism. But success did not alter his life; if anything, it compounded the pressures. Despite his freedoms, Meek had all the worries of an independent producer: without a regular outlet, each record had to be placed individually.

scenes.name: Antes del diluvio
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: La «edad oscura» del rock'n'roll: los rebeldes son sustituidos por ídolos adolescentes educados y el Brill Building devuelve el poder a los compositores profesionales. Pero en esos años se incuban la revolución futura: la guitarra fuzz de Link Wray, los bailes de moda (el twist), el rock instrumental de guitarras (Duane Eddy, Ventures, Shadows), el calipso y el primer ska, el doo-wop más inventivo (Coasters, Drifters, Five Royales), el nacimiento del soul (Sam Cooke, Ray Charles, Motown, Stax), el estudio como instrumento de Joe Meek y el surf de los Beach Boys y del «muro de sonido» de Phil Spector.

podcast.title: Murder-Suicide (February 3, 1967)
podcast.body: On February 3, 1967, the eighth anniversary of Buddy Holly's death, Joe Meek used a shotgun, owned by the bassist of The Tornados, to kill his landlady before taking his own life. "On February 3, 1967, which, by the way, just happened to be the eighth anniversary of Buddy Holly's death, he grabbed a few of his friends. To shotgun, owned by the base player of a band called the Tornados, killed his landlady and then himself."

podcast.title: Belief in Buddy Holly's Communication
podcast.body: Meek firmly believed that Buddy Holly, who had died in a plane crash in 1959, was speaking to him in his dreams. He also imagined that photographs in his studio would talk to him. "He believed that Buddy Holly, who had died in a plane crash in 1959, was speaking to him in his dreams."

srcs.episode: The Most Dangerous Artists in Rock

podcast.body: Joe Meek, a producer, worked with the band The Moon Trekkers, who later became Jimmy Powell and the Five Dimensions. Their collaboration included recording the song "Night of the Vampire." "had worked with Joe Meek recording Night of the Vampire."

podcast.title: Dealing with Landlady's Complaints
podcast.body: During recording sessions, when his landlady, Violet Shenton, would complain about the noise by banging on his ceiling with a broom, Meek would retaliate. His response was to place speakers on the stairwell and significantly increase the volume, aiming to annoy her further. "Durante esas grabaciones, cuando sus caseros creían que había hecho mucho ruido, golpeaban su techo con una espoba. El respondía poniendo los altavoces en las caleras, subiendo el volumen para molestar más."

srcs.episode: El productor que escuchó el nuevo mundo. Joe Meek.

podcast.title: Decline in Relevance post-Beatles
podcast.body: The meteoric rise and widespread popularity of The Beatles significantly impacted Joe Meek's career. After their emergence, his distinct productions began to be perceived as old-fashioned and outdated. His last number one hit was achieved in 1964. "Pero la fe de Pondos Beatles hizo que sus producciones fueran listas como antiguas y pasadas de moda. Su último número 1 lo lograría en 1964."

srcs.episode: El productor que escuchó el nuevo mundo. Joe Meek.

podcast.title: Disbelief in The Beatles' Talent
podcast.body: Prior to their global fame, Brian Epstein, a friend of Meek, presented a demo tape of a nascent band called The Beatles to Joe Meek, seeking his advice on whether to represent them. Meek famously dismissed their talent, advising Epstein not to pursue them. "Brian Epstein, amigo de Mick, demostró una maqueta de una banda que estaba empezando para pedirle consejos sobre si representarle sonó. La banda se llamaba Beatles, la respuesta de Mick fue que Nisemo le estáse."

srcs.episode: El productor que escuchó el nuevo mundo. Joe Meek.

podcast.title: Early Electronic Aptitude
podcast.body: Born in 1923 in Newwind, England, Joe Meek was said to have built the first television in his neighborhood as a child. He reportedly assembled it from electronic components scavenged from his neighbors' appliances, showcasing an early and undeniable talent for gadgets and electronics. "Se cuenta que Joe Mick nacido en 1923 en Newwind, en la Tierra, creó el primer televisor de su vecindario a base de componentes electrónicos que acumulaba de aparatos de sus vecinos cuando era tan solo un niño."

srcs.episode: El productor que escuchó el nuevo mundo. Joe Meek.

podcast.title: Further Delusions and Repressed Sexuality
podcast.body: In his final years, Joe Meek's psychotic delusions intensified. He refused to use the telephone, convinced that his landlady was listening to his calls and mentally controlling the musicians in his studio. This combination of commercial pressure, repressed sexuality, and profound paranoia severely impacted his already fragile mental health. "En sus últimos años, Mick empezó a experimentar de lídios psicóticos. Se negabó a usar el teléfono ya que creía que su casera escuchaba sus llamadas y controlaba la mente de los músicos del estudio."

srcs.episode: El productor que escuchó el nuevo mundo. Joe Meek.

podcast.title: Independent Producer Success
podcast.body: Despite operating as an independent producer, Joe Meek achieved remarkable success. He worked on 245 singles, with an impressive 45 of these reaching the Top 50 on the charts, a considerable feat for any independent producer. "Trabajó en 245 sencillos, 45 de los cuales alcanzaron el Top 50 para ser un productor independiente no está nada mal."

srcs.episode: El productor que escuchó el nuevo mundo. Joe Meek.

podcast.title: Innovative Recording Techniques
podcast.body: Meek was renowned for his unorthodox production methods, which included the exaggerated use of self-made compressors, direct bass input without an amplifier, sampling, and extensive overdubbing on one or two-track recorders to craft new and complex textures. He also utilized a distinctive technique of recording songs at slower speeds and then accelerating them during production to achieve his unique sound. "donde destacó por sus técnicas poportodoxas, como el uso exagerado de compresores que el mismo fabricaba, la entrada directa de bajo sin amplificador, el sampling, o el sobredoblaje en grabadoras de una o dos pistas para crear nuevas texturas."

srcs.episode: El productor que escuchó el nuevo mundo. Joe Meek.

podcast.title: Mental Health Deterioration and Paranoia
podcast.body: Joe Meek's mental health underwent a severe decline, leading him to experience psychotic delusions. He began to believe his flat was inhabited by poltergeists and that his mind was being controlled by extraterrestrials. In one instance, he furiously hung up on Phil Spector, accusing him of stealing his musical ideas, and was convinced that his landlady had installed microphones in his home with the same intention. "El deterioro de esos salud mental fue creciendo. Empezó a creer que en su piso había Paul Tergay's y que los extraterrestres controlaban su mente. En una ocasión recibió una llamada de Phil Spector, Mick le colgó un farado acusándole de robarle sus ideas."

srcs.episode: El productor que escuchó el nuevo mundo. Joe Meek.

podcast.title: Missed Opportunity with David Bowie
podcast.body: Joe Meek also famously passed on the opportunity to work with a very young David Bowie. This decision, along with others, highlighted that while Meek was a genius at recording, his ability to discover new musical talent was not his strong suit. "También dejo pasar la oportunidad de trabajar con un jovenquísimo David Bowie. Talento en las grabaciones les abraba, pero descubrir músicos no era su fuerte."

srcs.episode: El productor que escuchó el nuevo mundo. Joe Meek.

podcast.title: Missed Opportunity with Rod Stewart
podcast.body: Joe Meek once expressed interest in hiring a particular group but made it a condition that they dismiss their 16-year-old singer, Rod Stewart. Meek stated that he simply did not perceive any talent in the young vocalist. "En otra ocasión contrató un grupo con la condición de que se disiciaran de su cantante, al cual no le veía talento. Se trataba de rote stewar que tenía 16 años."

srcs.episode: El productor que escuchó el nuevo mundo. Joe Meek.

podcast.title: Modern Influence
podcast.body: Joe Meek's innovations were so influential and personal that many contemporary audio plugins and processors bear his name, serving as a direct testament to his lasting impact and the continued relevance of his unique recording techniques in modern music production. "Sus innovaciones fueron tan influyentes y personales que muchos plugins y procesadores de audio actuales llevan su nombre."

srcs.episode: El productor que escuchó el nuevo mundo. Joe Meek.

podcast.title: Murder-Suicide
podcast.body: On February 3, 1967, Joe Meek committed a tragic act, killing his landlady, Violet Shenton, before taking his own life. This devastating event followed an argument between them regarding noise levels and a significant amount of unpaid back rent that Meek owed her. "El 3 de febrero de 1967, Mick mataba su casera Vallele Chentón, luego un psiquito la vida. Ese día habían discutido por los niveles de ruido y por la cantidad del que le des atrasados que aún le bebía."

srcs.episode: El productor que escuchó el nuevo mundo. Joe Meek.

podcast.title: Non-Musician Producer
podcast.body: Despite his profound influence on music, Joe Meek famously could not play any instruments, nor could he read or write music. To compose, he would verbally convey his musical ideas, often by humming or singing, to a musician who would then interpret his precise directions. "Y todo ello, sin saber tocar un instrumento."

srcs.episode: El productor que escuchó el nuevo mundo. Joe Meek.

podcast.title: Obsession with Communicating with the Dead
podcast.body: Meek had a deep-seated obsession with communicating with the deceased. He would set up tape machines in cemeteries, hoping to record the voices of those who had passed on. "He had this thing about wanting to communicate with the dead."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Most Dangerous Artists in Rock

podcast.title: Obsession with the Dead and Occult
podcast.body: Joe Meek harbored a deep fascination with communicating with the dead. He would install tape recorders in cemeteries, hoping to capture voices from the afterlife, and once believed a cat's meow was a human-toned plea for help. He was also profoundly obsessed with Buddy Holly, who had died in a plane crash, claiming to communicate with him in dreams. "Amiglio fascinaba la idea de comunicarse con los muertos, instalaba grabadoras de cinta a los cementerios con la esperanza de capturar voces de ultratumba."

srcs.episode: El productor que escuchó el nuevo mundo. Joe Meek.

podcast.title: Paranoia and Landlady Dispute
podcast.body: Meek was particularly worried about his landlady, refusing to use the phone because he was positive she was eavesdropping. Meanwhile, his landlady was concerned about noise from his flat and studio, and he was behind on rent. "Meek was especially worried about his landlady."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Most Dangerous Artists in Rock

podcast.title: Pioneer of Electronic Rock
podcast.body: Joe Meek is widely acknowledged as the pioneer of electronic rock, revolutionizing the recording market from his home studio. He achieved this by inventing groundbreaking recording techniques and creating unique sonic universes that set him apart from his contemporaries. "Considerado por muchas como el pionero del rock electrónico, este hombre, desde su estudio casero, revolucionará al mercado discográfico creando nuevas técnicas de grabación y universos sonados únicos."

srcs.episode: El productor que escuchó el nuevo mundo. Joe Meek.

podcast.title: Posthumous Recognition
podcast.body: Following his death, Joe Meek's immense contributions to music largely faded into obscurity until the 1990s, when his figure as an innovative musician and producer began to be re-evaluated. In 2014, the English magazine NME (New Musical Express) named Meek the most important producer of all time, placing him above highly revered figures such as Phil Spector, Gwen Cillons (Glyn Johns), George Martin, and Rick Rubin. "Tras un muerte cayó en el olvido hasta los años 90, cuando empezaron a valorar su figura como músico y productor. En 2014, la revista inglesa a Neil Musical Express y leció a Mick como el productor más importante de todos los tiempos. Por encima de Phil Spector, Gwen Cillons, George Martin o Rick Rubin."

srcs.episode: El productor que escuchó el nuevo mundo. Joe Meek.

podcast.title: Production Company and Studio Location
podcast.body: Joe Meek established a production company initially named James Hound, which later became known as Mixville Sound. His studio was uniquely located within his residence, situated in a three-story building in London, directly above a leather shop. This shop was managed by his landlady, Violet Shenton, who also owned the property. "La sexta experiencia creó la empresa de producción de James Hound, más tarde conocida como Mixville Sound, la cual hubi con su vivienda, en un edificio de tres plantas en Londres sobre una tienda la cual estaba rejentada por Valle le Chentón, su casera."

srcs.episode: El productor que escuchó el nuevo mundo. Joe Meek.

podcast.title: RAF Radar Technician
podcast.body: During his military service, Joe Meek served as a radar technician in the Royal Air Force (RAF). This experience in electronics and technology further deepened his interest in both the field of electronics and the concept of space. "cuando hizo el servicio militar en la RAF, fue técnico en radar, documentos interés en la electrónica y el espacio."

srcs.episode: El productor que escuchó el nuevo mundo. Joe Meek.

podcast.title: Studio as an Instrument
podcast.body: Joe Meek was a trailblazer in using the recording studio itself as an instrument. He manipulated the studio's capabilities to shape and transform sounds and textures in highly innovative ways, effectively making the studio an integral part of the creative process, despite his own lack of formal musical training. "Pese a esa carencia, fue piano yero en usar el estudio de grabación como instrumento más."

srcs.episode: El productor que escuchó el nuevo mundo. Joe Meek.

podcast.title: Visionary Record Producer (Late 1950s-Early 1960s)
podcast.body: Joe Meek was one of the most visionary record producers in the world, known for pioneering techniques such as overdubs, reverb, sampling, and other outboard effects long before others adopted them. "Back in the late 50s and early 1960s, he was one of the most visionary record producers in the world."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Most Dangerous Artists in Rock

podcast.title: Worsening Mental Health and Illegal Sexuality
podcast.body: His mental health issues were exacerbated by the fact that he was gay, which was illegal in the UK at the time. This led to paranoia about being ruined through blackmail over his lifestyle. "His mental health issues worsened, spurred on by the fact that he was gay, something that was illegal in the UK at the time."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Most Dangerous Artists in Rock
